concepts.title: Limitation of CNNs: Locality vs Global Information

position.section_title: A Limitation of CNNs: Independence between Far Apart Patches

concepts.one_liner: CNNs are limited by their focus on locality, making it difficult to efficiently share global information across far apart image patches.
concepts.content:
CNNs are built around the idea of locality: different local regions of an image can safely be processed independently. This is what allows us to use filters with small kernels. However, very often, there is global information that needs to be shared across all receptive fields in an image. Convolutional layers are not well-suited to globalizing information since the only way they can do so is by either increasing the kernel size of their filters or stacking layers to increase the receptive field of neurons on deeper layers.

(see figure: Consider a 2-layer CNN with kernel size 3, tasked to compare $x_1$ and $x_7$. It can't do it: there are no neurons that are connected to both $x_1$ and $x_7$. Hatch marks indicate which neurons are...)

How can we efficiently pass messages across large spatial distances? We already have seen one option: just use a fully connected layer, so that every output neuron after this layer takes input from every neuron on the layer before. However, fully connected layers have a ton of parameters ($N^2$ if their input and output are $N$-dimensional vectors), and it can take an exorbitant amount of time and data to fit all those parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: While locality is efficient, many visual tasks require comparing distant parts of an image. CNNs struggle to do this without becoming computationally expensive or excessively deep.
concepts.recap_md:
- CNNs rely on local processing, which hinders the sharing of global information.
- Increasing receptive fields via stacking layers or larger kernels is inefficient.
- Fully connected layers solve the distance problem but introduce too many parameters.

concepts.title: The Idea of Attention
concepts.one_liner: Attention is a strategy for processing global information efficiently by focusing on the most salient parts of a signal.
concepts.content:
Attention is a strategy for processing global information efficiently, focusing just on the parts of the signal that are most salient to the task at hand. The idea can be motivated by attention in human perception. When we look at a scene, our eyes flick around and we attend to certain elements that stand out, rather than taking in the whole scene at once. If we are asked a question about the color of a car in the scene, we will move our eyes to look at the car, rather than just staring passively.

In neural nets, attention follows the same intuitive idea. A set of neurons on layer $l+1$ may attend to a set of neurons on layer $l$, in order to decide what their response should be. If we "ask" that set of neurons to report the color of any cars in the input image, then they should direct their attention to the neurons on the previous layer that represent the color of the car.
concepts.motivation_md: Attention allows a model to selectively process relevant information across large distances without the parameter explosion of fully connected layers.
concepts.recap_md:
- Mimics human perception by focusing on salient elements rather than the whole scene.
- Allows neurons to selectively "attend" to specific inputs from previous layers.
- Provides an efficient way to handle global information in neural networks.

concepts.title: Attention Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is a data-dependent matrix that allocates non-negative attention weights to each input.
concepts.content: The attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is a fundamental component of attention mechanisms. The important difference between $\mathbf{A}$ and a standard weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$ is that $\mathbf{A}$ is data-dependent; that is, the values of $\mathbf{A}$ are a function of the data input to the network. In addition, $\mathbf{A}$ typically only contains non-negative values, consistent with thinking of it as a matrix that allocates how much attention we pay to each input.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard neural network weights are fixed after training, but different inputs often require focusing on different parts of the data. The attention matrix allows the network to dynamically adjust its focus based on the specific input it is currently processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- The attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is data-dependent rather than fixed.
 - It typically consists of non-negative values.
 - It functions by allocating attention weights across the input data.

concepts.title: Dynamic Pooling
concepts.one_liner: Dynamic pooling is a form of mean pooling where weights are dynamically decided based on the input data.
concepts.content: Attention can be described as fully connected layers with data-dependent weights. Alternatively, attention can be viewed as a kind of dynamic pooling. This is similar to mean pooling but uses a weighted average where the weights are dynamically decided based on the input data.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard pooling operations like mean or max pooling treat all elements in a window the same way regardless of their content. Dynamic pooling allows the network to prioritize more relevant information within the pooling operation based on the input itself.
concepts.recap_md:
- Dynamic pooling is a weighted average pooling operation.
 - Weights are determined dynamically based on the input data.
 - It provides a different perspective on the attention mechanism.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention
concepts.one_liner: Query-key-value attention is the specific attention allocation function used in transformer architectures.
concepts.content: Query-key-value attention is the particular version of the attention allocation function $f$ that appears in transformers. It defines how attention is distributed across inputs by associating tokens with specific roles defined by queries, keys, and values.
concepts.motivation_md: To effectively retrieve information from a set of inputs, a system needs a way to specify what it is looking for (query), what each input contains (key), and what information should actually be extracted (value).
concepts.recap_md:
- It is the standard attention mechanism used in transformers.
 - It uses a specific allocation function $f$ to determine weights.
 - It relies on the interaction between queries, keys, and values.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Attention
concepts.one_liner: Transformers use query-key-value attention, where each token is associated with a query, a key, and a value vector.
concepts.content: Transformers use a particular kind of attention based on the idea of queries, keys, and values. In query-key-value attention, each token is associated with a query vector, a key vector, and a value vector. The idea of queries, keys, and values comes from databases, where a database cell holds a value, which is retrieved when a query matches the cell's key. Tokens are like database cells and attention is like retrieving information from the database of tokens. These vectors are defined as linear transformations of the token's code vector, projecting to query/key/value vectors of length $m$. For a token $\mathbf{t}$, we have: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{q} &= \mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ query}\\ \mathbf{k} &= \mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ key}\\ \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{W}_v \mathbf{t} \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ value} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This mechanism allows a model to selectively attend to relevant information by comparing a search criteria (query) against labels (keys) to extract content (values).
concepts.recap_md:
- Each token is transformed into query (q), key (k), and value (v) vectors.
 - Transformations are performed via learned weight matrices $\mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{W}_k, \mathbf{W}_v$.
 - It mimics database retrieval where a query matches a key to return a value.

concepts.title: Attention Layer Mechanics
concepts.one_liner: Attention mechanics involve matching query vectors against keys to compute weights for a weighted sum of value vectors.
concepts.content: In transformers, inputs are tokenized. For example, a textual question is represented as a token which submits its query vector, $\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}$, to be matched against the keys of other tokens (such as patches in an image). The similarity between the query and the key, most commonly measured by the dot product $\mathbf{q}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}$, determines the attention weight. Querying each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ results in a vector of similarities: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{s} = [s_1, \ldots, s_N]^\mathsf{T}&= [\mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{\texttt{question}}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_N]^\mathsf{T} \end{aligned}$$ We then normalize $\mathbf{s}$ using the softmax function to produce attention weights $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}$. Finally, we take a weighted sum over token value vectors to obtain the output $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{s})\\ \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \begin{bmatrix} a_1\mathbf{v}_1^\mathsf{T}\\ \vdots \\ a_N\mathbf{v}_N^\mathsf{T}\\ \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ [FIGURE:afb7764c48883324 | A legend showing the color coding for attention components: 'query' is represented by a yellow vertical rectangle, 'key' by a magenta vertical rectangle, and 'value' by a teal vertical rectangle.] (see figure: Mechanics of an attention layer. Queries from the question match keys from the tokens representing the impala; value vectors of the impala tokens then contribute the most to the sum that yields...)

 - Similarities are normalized via softmax to create a probability distribution of weights.
 - The final output is a weighted sum of value vectors.

concepts.title: Tokens as a Data Type
concepts.one_liner: A token is an encapsulated group of neurons, often represented as a vector, that serves as a fundamental data structure in deep learning.
concepts.content: A token is a fundamental data structure and group of neurons that can be viewed as a new data type. Unlike channels or batches, tokens are encapsulated groups of information where operators defined over them serve as the primary interface for accessing and modifying their internal contents. In this context, a token's internal content is a vector of neurons, represented by a column vector $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 1}$, which is also referred to as the token's code vector.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard neural networks operate on individual scalar neurons, many data types (like text or image patches) are naturally grouped. Treating these groups as "tokens"—encapsulated data types with their own defined operators—allows for more structured and expressive processing than treating every neuron independently.

concepts.title: Tokenizing Data
concepts.one_liner: Tokenization is the process of converting raw input data, such as image patches, into a set of vectors for processing by subsequent layers.
concepts.content:
The first step to working with tokens is to tokenize the raw input data. Once tokenized, all subsequent layers operate over tokens until the output layer makes a prediction. To tokenize an image, each patch of pixels is represented by a token. The token vector is either the vectorized patch (stacking color channels) or a lower-dimensional projection of that vectorized patch. Consequently, a full image corresponds to an array of tokens.

concepts.title: Matrix Representation of Tokens
concepts.one_liner: A sequence or set of tokens is represented by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, where each row is a transposed token vector.
concepts.content:
A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, where each token $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$ is transposed to become a row of the matrix:

$$\mathbf{T} = 
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots \\
    \mathbf{t}_N^\mathsf{T}\\
\end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: In this chapter, we will represent a set of tokens as a matrix whose rows are the token vectors.)

Transformers are invariant to permutations of the input sequence, so groups of tokens are effectively treated as sets rather than ordered sequences. This notation emphasizes that tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets; while an MLP takes a column vector of scalar neurons, a transformer operates over a matrix $\mathbf{T}$ representing an array of vector-valued tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing tokens as rows in a matrix allows us to use efficient linear algebra operations to process entire sets of data simultaneously. It also highlights the structural shift from scalar-based processing (MLPs) to vector-based processing (Transformers).

concepts.title: Mixing Tokens
concepts.one_liner: Mixing tokens involves taking a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens to produce new token representations.
concepts.content:
Mixing tokens is the operation of taking a linear combination of tokens. Unlike a fully connected layer in a standard neural net which takes a weighted sum of scalar neurons, this operation takes a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens.

(see figure: Linear combination of neurons versus tokens.)

The general equations for linear combinations of neurons versus tokens are:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{linear combination of neurons}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}&\quad\quad \triangleleft \quad \text{linear combination of tokens}
\end{aligned}$$

Operations over tokens are defined analogously to operations over neurons, with the primary difference being that tokens are vector-valued rather than scalar-valued.
concepts.motivation_md: To process information across different parts of an input (like different patches of an image), the model needs a way to combine information from multiple tokens. Linear mixing provides a fundamental mechanism for tokens to interact and share information.

concepts.title: Token Nets
concepts.one_liner: Token nets are computation graphs that use tokens as primary nodes, alternating between linear mixing layers and tokenwise nonlinearities.
concepts.content:
Token nets are computation graphs that use tokens as the primary nodes rather than individual neurons. They function similarly to neural nets by alternating between layers that mix nodes in linear combinations (such as fully connected or convolutional layers) and layers that apply pointwise nonlinearities (such as per-token MLPs). Because tokens are groups of neurons, a token net is essentially a neural net viewed as a "net of subnets."

(see figure: Neural nets versus token nets. The arrows here represent any functional dependency between the nodes (note that different arrows represent different types of functions).)

concepts.title: The Attention Layer
concepts.one_liner: An attention layer is a linear combination of tokens where the weights are dynamically determined by the input data rather than being fixed parameters.
concepts.content:
Attention layers define a special kind of linear combination of tokens using an attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ instead of a fixed weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$. The key distinction is that $\mathbf{A}$ is data-dependent; its values are a function $f$ of the input data. $\mathbf{A}$ typically contains non-negative values, representing the amount of "attention" paid to each input token.

(see figure: Fully-connected layers versus attention layers.)

The equation for an attention layer is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{A} &= f(\ldots) \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ attention}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}
\end{aligned}$$

Attention can be viewed as a form of dynamic pooling or a weighted average where weights are decided based on the input. For example, in an image query task, $f$ might assign high weights to tokens matching a specific text query (like "animal heads") and low weights to others. This allows the layer to dynamically change its behavior in response to different inputs.

(see figure: How attention can be allocated across different regions (tokens) in an image. The token code vectors consist of multiple dimensions and each can encode a different attribute of the token. To the left...)
concepts.motivation_md: Fixed weights in standard layers mean the model always looks at the same locations for information. Attention allows the model to focus on different parts of the input depending on the context, enabling it to answer specific queries or handle variable-length data more effectively.

concepts.one_liner: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set.

concepts.title: Self-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Self-attention is an architecture where every token in a layer submits a query and computes a weighted sum over all other tokens in that same layer.
concepts.content:
Self-attention is a generic architecture where we don't have to hand-design which tokens interact in which ways. The idea is that on a self-attention layer, *all* tokens submit queries, and for each of these queries, we take a weighted sum over *all* tokens in that layer. If $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ is a set of $N$ input tokens, then we have $N$ queries, $N$ weighted sums, and $N$ output tokens to form $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. This is visualized below in @fig-transformers-self_attn_layer.

(see figure: A self-attention layer.)

concepts.title: Intuition of Self-Attention
concepts.one_liner: Self-attention allows tokens to refine their representations by aggregating context from other relevant tokens, such as grouping patches of the same object in an image.
concepts.content:
The intuition of self-attention is that it's easier to recognize a patch given the context of other relevant patches around it. For example, in semantic segmentation, a token $\mathbf{t}_2$ representing an impala torso can be updated by attending to other impala patches to refine its representation into a more abstracted vector capturing the label *impala*. This refinement sums over token code vectors, reducing noise and amplifying commonalities. Further, a query could retrieve information from related context, such as giraffe or zebra patches, which provide informative biome context.

(see figure: One way self-attention could be used to aggregate information across all patches containing the same object, and thereby arrive at a better representation of the object in $\mathbf{t}_2$, the query...)

Actual usage is determined by training data. Tokens on hidden layers do not necessarily represent spatially localized patches; attention layers can mix information across spatially distant tokens, meaning $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}[0,:]$ may not represent the same spatial region as $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]$.

(see figure: Example of self-attention maps where each token is an image patch and the query and key vectors are both set to the mean color of the patch, normalized to be a unit vector.)

concepts.title: Multihead Self-Attention (MSA)
concepts.one_liner: Multihead self-attention runs multiple attention layers in parallel to capture different types of token similarities simultaneously.
concepts.content:
A single self-attention layer measures similarity in just one way, defined by the matrix $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}_k$. To measure similarity in multiple ways (e.g., color, texture, and shape), transformers use **multihead self-attention** (**MSA**), which runs $k$ attention layers in parallel on the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. The $k$ outputs are concatenated and projected back to the original dimensionality:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^i &= \texttt{attn}^i(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}) \quad \text{for } i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}\\
    \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} &= \begin{bmatrix}
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[0,:] & \ldots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[0,:]\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
        \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1[N-1,:] & \ldots & \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k[N-1,:]\\
    \end{bmatrix}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$ is a learnable matrix that merges the heads. Unlike single-headed attention, the value vectors in MSA do not need to match the token code dimensionality because of this final projection. MSA allows for adding parallel complexity, complementary to adding sequential depth.

concepts.title: Token Normalization
concepts.one_liner: Token normalization standardizes the dimensions of each individual token code vector using its own mean and variance.
concepts.content: This architecture uses layer normalization before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is performed *within* each token: the token code vector is treated akin to a layer, and each dimension of this vector is standardized by the mean and variance over all its dimensions. This `token norm` is a tokenwise operation without learnable parameters. Residual connections are typically added around these layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing within each token helps stabilize training and ensures that the scale of features remains consistent across the network's layers.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance of Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Transformers are permutation equivariant, meaning scrambling the input token order results in an identically scrambled output order.
concepts.content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are **permutation equivariant**:

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ reorders the rows of the matrix. Since the full transformer is a composition of these layers (along with residual connections and token normalization, which are also equivariant), the entire architecture is permutation equivariant:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.)
concepts.motivation_md: This property reflects that the basic attention mechanism treats the input as a set rather than a sequence, making it naturally flexible for data where order might be arbitrary or should be handled explicitly.

concepts.title: Layer Selection Based on Symmetries
concepts.one_liner: Selecting neural network layers that reflect the symmetries of the data, such as translation or permutation equivariance, is a key architectural strategy.
concepts.content: A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task. For example, in object detection, translation equivariance is useful because an object's identity remains the same regardless of its location. Permutation equivariance is also relevant, though scrambling image patches can disrupt spatial layout important for recognition. Transformers address this by using positional codes to reinsert spatial information into the permutation-equivariant architecture.

concepts.title: Attention Layers vs. Convolutional Layers
concepts.one_liner: Attention layers perform global operations where all input tokens can interact, unlike convolutional layers which are restricted to local receptive fields.
concepts.content: Attention layers are not convolutional. They do not factor the processing into independent chunks but instead perform a global operation, in which all input tokens can interact. The linear combination of tokens that results is not a mixing operation found in CNNs and addresses the limitation of CNNs being myopic, with each filter only seeing information in its receptive field.
concepts.motivation_md: Convolutional layers are limited by their local receptive fields, making them "myopic." Attention layers solve this by allowing global interactions between all tokens in a sequence or image.

concepts.title: Masked Attention
concepts.one_liner: Masked attention restricts which tokens can attend to others by fixing specific weights in the attention matrix to zero.
concepts.content:
Sometimes we want to restrict which tokens can attend to which. This can be done by masking the attention matrix, which just means fixing some of the weights to be zero. This can be useful for many settings, including learning features via masked autoencoding, cross-attention between different data modalities, and for sequential prediction. 

To illustrate, we will describe the sequential prediction use case. For simplicity, in this section we depict tokens with one-dimensional code vectors, but remember $\mathbf{T}$ would have $d$ columns for $d$-dimensional code vectors. A common problem is to predict the $(n+1)$-th token in a sequence given the previous $n$ tokens. For example, we may be trying to predict tokens that represent the next frame in a video, the next word in a sentence, or the weather on the next day. The $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$ is shorthand for the sequence of tokens $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{t}_{n}^\mathsf{T} \end{bmatrix}$.

A simple way to model this prediction problem is with a linear layer: $\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$. Here is what this looks like diagrammatically, and on the right is the layer shown as matrix multiplication:

(see figure: Masked prediction of time index 4 from time indices 1-3.)

During training, we will give examples like this: $$\begin{aligned} \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_n\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n+1}\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-1}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_n\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-2}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n-1} \end{aligned}$$ and so on. We can make all these predictions at once with a single matrix multiply:

(see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.)

This way, one forward pass makes $N$ predictions rather than one prediction. This is equivalent to doing a single next token prediction $N$ times, but it all happens in a single matrix multiply, using the matrix shown on the right.
concepts.motivation_md: Masking is used to control information flow, such as preventing a model from 'cheating' by looking at future tokens during sequential prediction or for specific tasks like masked autoencoding.

This can be useful for many settings, including learning features via masked autoencoding, cross-attention between different data modalities, and for sequential prediction. 

To illustrate, we will describe the sequential prediction use case. For simplicity, in this section we depict tokens with one-dimensional code vectors, but remember $\mathbf{T}$ would have $d$ columns for $d$-dimensional code vectors. A common problem is to predict the $(n+1)$-th token in a sequence given the previous $n$ tokens. For example, we may be trying to predict tokens that represent the next frame in a video, the next word in a sentence, or the weather on the next day. The $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$ is shorthand for the sequence of tokens $\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{t}_{n}^\mathsf{T} \end{bmatrix}$.

A simple way to model this prediction problem is with a linear layer: $\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$. Here is what this looks like diagrammatically, and on the right is the layer shown as matrix multiplication:

(see figure: Masked prediction of time index 4 from time indices 1-3.)

During training, we will give examples like this: $$\begin{aligned} \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_n\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n+1}\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-1}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_n\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-2}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n-1} \end{aligned}$$ and so on. We can make all these predictions at once with a single matrix multiply:

(see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.)

This way, one forward pass makes $N$ predictions rather than one prediction. This is equivalent to doing a single next token prediction $N$ times, but it all happens in a single matrix multiply, using the matrix shown on the right.

concepts.title: Causal Attention
concepts.one_liner: Causal attention is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in a sequence.
concepts.content: This kind of matrix is called causal because each output index $i$ only depends on input indices $j$ such that $j < i$. If $\mathbf{A}$ is an attention matrix, then this strategy is called causal attention. This is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence. This approach can dramatically speed up training because all the sub-sequence prediction problems (predict $\mathbf{t}_{n-1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-2}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-1}$, predict $\mathbf{t}_{n+1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$) are supervised at the same time.
concepts.motivation_md: In sequential tasks, we must ensure the model does not use information from the future to predict the present. Causal attention enforces this constraint while allowing parallel training on all prefixes of a sequence.

concepts.title: Multilayer Masked Attention
concepts.one_liner: Multilayer masked attention maintains causal dependencies across deep networks by sharing computation between overlapping prediction sub-networks.
concepts.content: This also works for transformers with more than one layer, where the masking strategy looks like shown in (see figure: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction with a deep net.). concepts.title: Positional Encodings
concepts.one_liner: Positional encodings concatenate a code representing a token's position within a signal to retain spatial or sequential knowledge.
concepts.content:
Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes. A consequence is that tokens do not encode their position within the representation of the signal. Sometimes, however, we may wish to retain positional knowledge. For example, knowing that a token is a representation of the top region of an image can help us identify that the token is likely to represent sky. 

Positional encoding concatenates a code representing position within the signal onto each token. If the signal is an image, then the positional code should represent the x- and y-coordinates. However, it need not represent these coordinates as scalars; more commonly we use a periodic representation of position, where the coordinates are encoded as the vector of values a set of sinusoidal waves take on at each position: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{p}_x &= [\sin(x), \sin(x/B), \sin(x/B^2), \ldots, \sin(x/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p}_y &= [\sin(y), \sin(y/B), \sin(y/B^2), \ldots, \sin(y/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p} &= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}_x\\ \mathbf{p}_y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ where $x$ and $y$ are the coordinates of the token. This representation is visualized in (see figure: Positional codes.). 

Another strategy is to simply let the positional codes be learned by the model, which could potentially result in a better representation of space than sinusoidal codes. While positional encoding is useful and common in transformers, it is not specific to this architecture. The same kind of encodings can be useful for CNNs as well, as a way to make convolutional filters that are conditioned on position. Positional encodings also appear in radiance fields.
concepts.motivation_md: Because transformer operations are permutation equivariant, they are 'position-blind.' Positional encodings are necessary to give the model information about where tokens are located in a sequence or image.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance in Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, meaning shuffling input positions only permutes the outputs without changing the underlying computation.
concepts.content: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes (the only change is that the outputs get permuted). A consequence is that tokens do not encode their position within the representation of the signal. This property explains why transformers require additional mechanisms, like positional encodings, if the order or location of data points is important for the task.

concepts.title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

position.section_title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

concepts.one_liner: Fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers are all affine transformations that differ in how their weight matrices are structured and determined.
concepts.content:
Many layers in deep nets are special kinds of affine transformations. Three common types are fully-connected layers (`fc`), convolutional layers (`conv`), and self-attention layers (`attn`). All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$. 

In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as some function of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `conv` layers this function is very simple: just make a Toeplitz matrix that repeats the convolutional kernel(s) to match the dimensionality of $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. In `attn` layers the function that determines $\mathbf{W}$ is more involved, and typically biases $\mathbf{b}$ are not used. 

Each of these layers can be represented as a matrix. The matrix for an `fc` layer is full rank, whereas the matrices for `conv` and `attn` layers have low-rank structure, but different kinds of low-rank structure. (see figure: A comparison of three neural network layer types: fully connected (fc), convolutional (conv), and self-attention (attn). For each, it shows a wiring graph of connections between input and output...) catalog some of the other important properties of each of these layers.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding different layer types as variations of affine transformations helps unify deep learning theory and highlights how architectural constraints (like weight sharing in CNNs or input-dependency in Attention) affect the model's capacity.

concepts.title: Transformers as Graph Neural Networks
concepts.one_liner: Transformers can be viewed as a special case of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that process sets of tokens by forming a graph of operations.
concepts.content:
Transformers are the dominant architecture in computer vision and most fields of artificial intelligence. They combine ideas from earlier architectures—convolutional patchwise processing, residual connections, ReLU nonlinearities, and normalization layers—with newer innovations like vector-valued tokens, attention layers, and positional codes. 

Transformers can also be considered as a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs). GNNs are a very general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer does exactly that: it takes an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applies a network of transformations over that set until a final representation or prediction is read out.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing transformers as GNNs provides a theoretical framework for understanding how they process unstructured sets of data through relational operations rather than just fixed grids or sequences.

concepts.title: Tokenization as Convolution
concepts.one_liner: Tokenization can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to the patch size $K$.
concepts.content:
The first step in working with transformers is to tokenize the input. The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. This operation can be written as convolution; the whole idea of CNNs is to chop the signal into patches. In particular, this form of tokenization can be written as a convolutional layer with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{T}[n(N/K)+m,c_{\texttt{2}}] = \nonumber\\
&b[c_{\texttt{2}}] +  \sum_{c_{\texttt{1}}=1}^{C_{\texttt{in}}} \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[c_{\texttt{1}},c_{\texttt{2}},k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},K n-k_1,K m-k_2] \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{(tokenization)}
\end{aligned}$$
where, for RGB images, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$, $C_{\texttt{in}}=3$, and $C_{\texttt{out}}=d$ (the token dimensionality). This math assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$; if they aren't then the input can be resized or padded until they are. This is just a $\texttt{conv}$ operator with the following parameters:

```python
T = conv(x_in, channels_in=3, channels_out=d, kernel=K, stride=K) # tokenize
```

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Projections as Convolutions
concepts.one_liner: The query, key, and value projections in transformers are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
concepts.content:
The query, key, and value projections that are part of the attention layers can be viewed as convolutions. For simplicity, consider the query projection, since key and value follow the same pattern. This operation is typically written as a matrix multiply $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}$, which applies the same linear transformation ($\mathbf{W}_q$) to each token vector. Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized below:

(see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.)

Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.

concepts.title: Similarities between CNNs and Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Most layers in transformers are convolutional, breaking the signal into chunks and processing them independently and identically.
concepts.content: Most layers in transformers are convolutional. These layers break up the signal processing problem into chunks, then process each chunk independently and identically. concepts.title: Permutation Invariance and 1x1 Filters in Transformers
concepts.one_liner: Transformers use $1 \times 1$ filters to maintain permutation invariance, unlike CNNs which use larger kernels to process adjacent regions together.
concepts.content: When written as convolutions, the query-key-value projections and token-wise MLPs in transformers only use $1 \times 1$ filters. This is necessary because using a larger kernel would break the permutation invariance property of transformers; the output of the filters would depend on which token is next to which. This is a key difference between CNNs and transformers: CNNs use $K \times K$ filters to process adjacent image regions together, while transformers use $1 \times 1$ filters and have no architectural way of knowing about spatial structure.
